text: John II (French: Jean II; 26 April 1319 – 8 April 1364), known as John the Good, ruled as King of France from 1350 until his death in 1364. Upon ascending the throne, France faced severe crises: the Black Death, which killed between a third and a half of its population; widespread popular revolts known as Jacqueries; the activities of free companies (Grandes Compagnies) of routiers who plundered the country; and sustained English aggression, culminating in the catastrophic Battle of Poitiers in 1356, where John was captured. While imprisoned in London, his son Charles served as regent and suppressed several rebellions before concluding the Treaty of Brétigny in 1360, which resulted in France losing significant territories and paying a massive ransom. As part of an exchange of hostages, including his son Louis I, Duke of Anjou, John was released to raise funds for the ransom. Upon returning to France, he introduced the franc to stabilize the currency and attempted to eliminate the free companies by sending them on a crusade, though Pope Innocent VI died before the meeting in Avignon. When informed that Louis had escaped captivity, John voluntarily returned to England, where he died in 1364 and was succeeded by his eldest son, Charles V. John was nine years old when his father, Philip VI, became king; Philip’s succession was unexpected because all three sons of Philip IV had died without male heirs and their daughters were passed over, as was King Edward III of England, Philip IV’s granddaughter through Isabella. To secure his throne, Philip married off his son John at age thirteen to King John the Blind of Bohemia, who sought French support for controlling Lombardy. A treaty was signed, stipulating that Bohemia would provide four hundred infantrymen in war and that the Lombard crown would not be contested if Bohemia obtained it. Bonne of Bohemia, selected as John’s wife due to her child-bearing age (16 years), brought a dowry of 120,000 florins. John reached the age of majority on 27 April 1332 and was granted the Duchy of Normandy, along with the counties of Anjou and Maine. The wedding took place on 28 July at Notre-Dame in Melun, attended by six thousand guests, and was followed by a two-month celebration culminating in his knighting at Notre-Dame in Paris. As duke, he was formally granted knightly arms before a gathering of European monarchs and dukes. Upon becoming duke, John faced the reality that most Norman nobility were aligned with England, as Normandy relied heavily on maritime trade across the English Channel. To maintain stability, Norman nobles were organized into interdependent clans with charters ensuring autonomy, primarily divided between the counts of Tancarville and Harcourt. In 1341, tensions flared when Geoffroy d'Harcourt raised troops against King Philip, demanding he be made duke to secure autonomy; royal forces captured Saint-Sauveur-le-Vicomte and exiled Geoffroy, with three of his companions decapitated in Paris on 3 April 1344. In 1342, John was in Avignon for the coronation of Pope Clement VI, and in 1343, he participated in peace negotiations with Edward III’s chancery clerk. By 1345, increasing numbers of Norman rebels defected to Edward III, threatening royal legitimacy. The French defeat at Crécy on 26 August 1346 and the fall of Calais on 3 August 1347 further damaged royal prestige. In response, Philip VI sought a truce, and John negotiated with Geoffroy d'Harcourt, agreeing to return confiscated goods and appointing him sovereign captain in Normandy. He then allied with the Tancarville family by marrying John, Viscount of Melun, to Jeanne, heiress of Tancarville, ensuring loyalty to John while allowing Geoffroy to continue defending Norman autonomy. On 11 September 1349, John’s wife, Bonne of Bohemia, died at Maubuisson Abbey from the Black Death. To escape the pandemic, John left Paris. On 9 February 1350, five months after her death, he married Joan I, Countess of Auvergne, at the Château de Sainte-Gemme near Saint-Germain-en-Laye. In 1343, negotiations began between Philip VI and dauphin Humbert II of Viennois over the inheritance of the Dauphiné, initially assigning it to John’s younger brother Philip, Duke of Orléans, but later changed to John as heir. By 1349, Humbert relinquished the Dauphiné to the House of Valois, designating John’s eldest son Charles as successor, with the condition that Dauphiné remain a distinct polity. Thus, in 1349, Charles became the first Valois Dauphin de Viennois, and in 1350, upon John’s coronation as king, Charles became heir presumptive, holding both the title of Dauphin de Viennois and the right to the French throne. Philip VI died on 22 August 1350, and John was crowned king of France on 26 September 1350 in Reims, with his second wife, Joanna, crowned queen at the same time. In November 1350, John had Raoul II of Brienne, Count of Eu, seized and executed, though the reasons remain unclear, with rumors suggesting he had pledged the County of Guînes for his release. John inherited a militarily disorganized and fragmented kingdom, and seven months after his coronation, he issued the ordinances of 1351 to address military issues, including poor organization, discipline, and payment, in response to defeats like Crécy. These ordinances are considered the first comprehensive military reforms in French history, surpassing earlier decrees by focusing systematically on army-wide structure. The reforms aimed to counter the English armies’ use of longbowmen and centralized command. However, resistance from the nobility—such as Charles of Navarre—undermined implementation, as they viewed the reforms as a threat to their feudal autonomy and traditional rights to command personal forces. Rivalries among noble factions, including Charles of Navarre and the Duke of Orléans, caused political instability and weakened royal authority. Nobles resisted discipline and resented serving under royal oversight or alongside common soldiers, leading to inconsistent enforcement and reliance on feudal levies with irregular payments. The failure to integrate these reforms contributed to the French defeat at Poitiers. The battle exposed military weaknesses and highlighted noble resistance, leading to the Treaty of Brétigny (1360), which ceded territories to England (later recovered by Charles V) and caused thousands of French casualties, including nobles, further weakening the feudal structure. Although the ordinances were limited in effectiveness due to enforcement challenges and financial constraints, they laid the foundation for modernizing the French military, influencing later reforms by Charles V and Charles VII, including the creation of a standing army and permanent taxation. These changes transformed the feudal system from decentralized to one with royal oversight, integrating nobles into a royal framework and strengthening crown authority. On 16 November 1351, John established the Order of the Star, a chivalric order designed to unify the French nobility under royal leadership and counter Edward III’s Order of the Garter. Unlike religious military orders such as the Templars or Hospitallers, the Order of the Star was a royal, state-sponsored initiative with a clear military purpose tied to national defense, making it the first organized, state-backed knightly group in France. It aimed to foster loyalty among knights and prevent defections to foreign powers, especially among nobles with lands across multiple kingdoms. In 1354, John’s son-in-law and cousin, Charles II of Navarre, who held lands in Normandy and the Kingdom of Navarre, was implicated in the assassination of the Constable of France, Charles de la Cerda, John’s favorite. To secure a strategic ally against the English in Gascony, John signed the Treaty of Mantes on 22 February 1354. The peace was short-lived, and Charles eventually allied with Henry of Grosmont, the first Duke of Lancaster. In September 1355, John and Charles signed the Treaty of Valognes, but it lasted only briefly. On 5 April 1356, during a banquet at the Royal Castle in Rouen attended by John’s son Charles, John burst through the door in full armor, swords drawn, with over a hundred fully armed knights, shouting, “Let no one move if he does not want to be dead with this sword.” When Charles of Navarre and other nobles refused to comply, John grabbed him by the throat, yelling, “Traitor, you are not worthy to sit at my son's table!” He then ordered the arrest of all guests, and later that night, summarily executed John, Count of Harcourt, and several other Norman lords and notables while standing nearby—an act driven by revenge for the assassination of Charles de la Cerda. This action alienated remaining Norman support from the crown, pushing many lords to align with Edward III and the English, setting the stage for the English invasion and the Battle of Poitiers. In 1355, the Hundred Years' War flared again, and in July 1356, Edward, the Black Prince, launched a chevauchée through France. John pursued him with his own army, meeting him a few miles southeast of Poitiers in September. John believed his army was twice the size of the English force and did not immediately attack. While waiting, papal legates attempted to negotiate a truce; the Black Prince offered his wagon train, promised not to fight for seven years, and even offered to return Calais to France. John demanded 100 of the Prince’s best knights as hostages, including the Prince himself. No agreement was reached, and combat began. On the day of battle, John and 17 knights from his personal guard dressed identically to confuse the enemy. Despite this, the French knights were routed by English longbow volleys, and John was captured as the English force advanced. Though he fought valiantly with a large battle-axe and his helmet was knocked off, he surrendered when Denis de Morbecque, a French exile fighting for England, approached him and offered to lead him to the Prince of Wales. John surrendered by handing him his glove. That night, he dined in the Black Prince’s red silk tent, who attended to him personally. He was then taken to Bordeaux and then to England. The Battle of Poitiers was one of the most significant military disasters in medieval history for France. While negotiating peace, John was held first in the Savoy Palace, then in Windsor, Hertford, Somerton Castle in Lincolnshire, Berkhamsted Castle in Hertfordshire, and briefly at King John’s Lodge in East Sussex, before being transferred to the Tower of London. In France, the public reaction was not to the defeat at Poitiers but to the captivity of King John. When people learned of the French lords’ flight from battle, they believed it was due to treason. They questioned the meaning of honor and nobility, and some returning nobles were attacked by furious villeins, even those who had been on parole to collect ransoms. As a prisoner of the English, John was granted royal privileges that permitted him to maintain certain rights.

King John II of France was a central figure in one of the major military disasters of the Middle Ages, particularly due to his capture at the Battle of Poitiers in 1356. After being taken prisoner by the English, he was held in various locations including the Savoy Palace, Windsor, Hertford, Somerton Castle in Lincolnshire, Berkhamsted Castle in Hertfordshire, and briefly at King John's Lodge in East Sussex, before being transferred to the Tower of London. In France, the public reaction to his captivity overshadowed the defeat at Poitiers, as people believed the French lords’ flight was due to treason and cowardice, leading to widespread hatred of knights perceived as treacherous. Despite being a prisoner, John was granted royal privileges allowing him to travel and maintain a regal lifestyle, during which his account books show he purchased horses, pets, clothes, and maintained an astrologer and court band. The Treaty of Brétigny, drafted in May 1360, set his ransom at 3 million crowns—roughly two to three years of France’s national revenue, the largest budget in Europe at the time. On 30 June 1360, John left the Tower of London and went to Eltham Palace, where Queen Philippa hosted a farewell entertainment; he spent the night in Dartford, stopped at the Maison Dieu of St Mary at Ospringe, paid homage at St Thomas Becket’s shrine in Canterbury on 4 July, dined with the Black Prince at Dover Castle, and reached Calais on 8 July. Leaving his son Louis of Anjou in Calais as a hostage to ensure payment, John was allowed to return to France to raise the ransom, and the treaty was ratified in October 1360. On 1 July 1363, John learned that Louis had escaped from Calais, prompting him to voluntarily return to England in January 1364 to negotiate with Edward III in person, despite opposition from his advisors. He famously stated that “if good faith were banned from the Earth, she ought to find asylum in the hearts of kings.” Immediately after, he appointed his son Charles as Duke of Normandy and regent of France. John landed in England in January 1364, was met by Sir Alan Buxhull, Sir Richard Pembridge, and Lord Burghersh at Dover, and was taken to Eltham and the Savoy Palace, where he was warmly received and a frequent guest of Edward at Westminster. A few months later, he fell ill with an unknown malady and died at the Savoy Palace in April 1364. His body was returned to France and interred in the royal chambers at Saint Denis Basilica. John’s death at age 44 was not unusually young for the period, especially considering the impact of the Black Death and the stresses of captivity. Primary sources, including Jean Froissart and the Grandes Chroniques de France, do not specify the nature of his illness, only noting he “fell ill and died,” and neither describe him as frail or chronically unwell. Froissart’s account of John’s lavish lifestyle in captivity and his participation in festivities suggests physical capability, while his preference for hunting over jousting and reliance on advisors like Charles de la Cerda may reflect personal temperament or political strategy rather than illness. The claim of poor health is largely a modern historiographical construct based on inferences, not direct evidence. John II married Bonne of Bohemia and had 11 children in eleven years. His close relationship with Charles de la Cerda, who was appointed connetable and accompanied him on journeys, drew criticism from partisans of Charles II of Navarre, who accused him of having “no other God than him”; La Cerda was later stabbed to death in 1354, an event that deeply grieved John. John acquired the titles of Count of Anjou, Count of Maine, and Duke of Normandy in 1332, which were later absorbed into the royal domain upon his coronation in 1350. During his reign, he created seven duchies and counties—the most of any French monarch—expanding French territory and influence by acquiring the Duchy of Burgundy, creating the Duchy of Auvergne, and placing his sons in strategic positions. He elevated the Barony of Tancarville to a county and created Jean, Viscount of Melun, as Count of Tancarville, who served as Chamberlain, Hereditary Constable of Normandy, Sovereign Master of the Waters and Forests of France, and held key military roles, including a lieutenancy general in 1361 to pacify regions threatened by the Free Companies. He also elevated Castres to a county in 1356 and granted it to John VI of Vendôme, a loyal vassal who fought at Poitiers and was captured by the English, as a reward and to secure loyalty in a region vulnerable to English influence. In 1360, the Duchy of Anjou was created and granted to Louis I of Anjou, John’s second son, as part of the Treaty of Brétigny, to secure a loyal presence in a region near English-held Aquitaine and Brittany, with Louis serving as a hostage in England. Philip II the Bold initially received Touraine as an apanage in 1360, but after Burgundy became available in 1363, Philip was given Burgundy instead, and Touraine was temporarily reassigned or returned to the crown, reflecting John’s strategic flexibility. The Duchy of Auvergne was created from the Terre royale d’Auvergne and granted to John’s third son, John, alongside the Duchy of Berry, to strengthen royal control in a region with a history of autonomy and pro-English sympathies. John served as king’s lieutenant in Auvergne since 1358, making him a logical recipient of the apanage. John II was succeeded by his eldest son, Charles, who became Charles V, known as The Wise.

King John created the Duchy of Berry for his third son, John, encompassing the County of Berry and parts of Poitou, as part of his 1360 reorganization of apanages following the Treaty of Brétigny. Centered in central France, Berry was a relatively stable region strategically important for connecting northern and southern royal domains and serving as a buffer against internal dissent, such as the Jacquerie revolt (1358). John of Berry, appointed king’s lieutenant in 1358 for regions including Auvergne and Languedoc, was a key figure in John’s government, and the apanage provided him with the resources to govern effectively and support royal policies. Unlike Anjou or Burgundy, Berry was less exposed to immediate external threats, making it a stable base for administrative and artistic patronage. John of Berry became a renowned patron of the arts, commissioning works like the Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry. His governance strengthened royal influence in central France, with Berry remaining closely tied to the crown. The Duchy of Auvergne was created from the Terre royale d’Auvergne (royal lands of Auvergne), while the County of Auvergne continued to exist in parallel. John granted it to his third son John alongside the Duchy of Berry. Auvergne, in south-central France, had been part of the royal domain since its confiscation by Philip II Augustus in 1209 and partial restoration to local counts. The elevation of Auvergne to a duchy was a strategic move to strengthen royal control in a region with a history of autonomy and pro-English sympathies among some local lords (e.g., the Counts of Auvergne). By granting it to John, King John aimed to secure Auvergne’s loyalty during the Hundred Years’ War. John’s role as king’s lieutenant in Auvergne (since 1358) made him a logical choice for the apanage. The grant formalized his authority, countering local resistance and English influence in the region. The creation of the duchy alongside Berry reflects John’s intent to consolidate central and southern France under a trusted son, especially after the territorial losses of the Treaty of Brétigny. John of Berry held Auvergne until his death in 1416, when it reverted to the crown. His daughter Marie inherited the title of Duchess of Auvergne, and it later passed to her husband, John I, Duke of Bourbon, in 1426, integrating Auvergne into the Bourbon domains. The apanage reinforced royal authority in Auvergne, though John’s heavy taxation to fund war efforts sparked revolts, such as the Tuchin Revolt, highlighting the challenges of governing the region. Touraine later became an apanage for other royal relatives under John’s successors, reinforcing its role as a “floating” apanage for royal cadets. On 28 July 1332, at the age of 13, John was married to Bonne of Luxembourg (d. 1349), daughter of John, King of Bohemia. On 19 February 1350, at the royal Château de Sainte-Gemme, John married Joanna I of Auvergne (d. 1361), Countess of Auvergne and Boulogne. Joanna was the widow of Philip of Burgundy, the deceased heir of that duchy, and the mother of the young Philip I, Duke of Burgundy (1344–61), who became John's stepson and ward. John and Joanna had three children, all of whom died shortly after birth. King John II faced extraordinary challenges: the Black Death, which killed a third to half of France’s population, the Hundred Years’ War with England, internal revolts like the Jacquerie, and plundering by free companies. His capture at the Battle of Poitiers (1356) and the subsequent Treaty of Brétigny (1360), which ceded significant territories and demanded a massive ransom, have often been focal points for criticism. However, applying modern standards of leadership to a medieval monarch risks oversimplifying the political, economic, and social constraints of the era. The trend of criticizing John II began with Jean Froissart’s influential but biased chronicle, which provided a narrative of bravery undercut by recklessness. Jules Michelet’s 19th-century reinterpretation transformed this into a nationalist critique, portraying John as a weak ruler who failed France. Subsequent historians—François Guizot, Charles Petit-Dutaillis, Edouard Perroy, Jean Deviosse, and Maurice Keen—built on Michelet’s framework, citing each other and Froissart to reinforce a narrative of incompetence. This historiographical chain reflects a tendency to judge John II by modern standards of statecraft, often ignoring the medieval emphasis on chivalric honor and the external pressures of war, plague, and noble factionalism. The reliance on citations created an echo chamber, where each historian reinforced the previous one’s conclusions without fully reevaluating primary sources like Jean de Venette or considering the broader context. Modern scholars like Françoise Autrand have begun to break this cycle by highlighting John II’s adherence to chivalric ideals and the impossible circumstances he faced, suggesting that the trend of criticism may be waning as historians adopt a more contextual approach. The earliest significant criticism of John II likely stems from contemporary or near-contemporary chroniclers, particularly Jean Froissart (c. 1337–c. 1405), a Hainaut-born chronicler whose Chronicles are a primary source for the Hundred Years’ War. Froissart’s account, while vivid and detailed, often reflects a chivalric bias and the perspective of his patrons, who included figures aligned with the English or Burgundian factions. His portrayal of John II at Poitiers emphasizes the king’s bravery but also his tactical errors, such as ignoring advice against engaging the English due to their superior longbow tactics. Froissart writes of John’s decision to fight on foot with a poleaxe, portraying it as courageous but implying it was reckless given the French defeat. This narrative sets a tone of personal valor undermined by poor judgment, a theme later historians amplified. Froissart’s account was influential because it was widely circulated in medieval Europe and became a foundational source for later historians. His depiction of John II’s capture and lavish lifestyle in English captivity—engaging in feasts, hunting, and pilgrimages—contributed to perceptions of a king more concerned with personal honor than governance. While Froissart does not explicitly condemn John, his focus on the king’s extravagance and military failure provided raw material for subsequent criticism. Another contemporary source, Jean de Venette (c. 1307–c. 1370), a Carmelite friar, offers a more sympathetic view, emphasizing the external pressures John faced, such as the Black Death and economic collapse. However, Venette’s chronicle was less widely read than Froissart’s, so it had less impact on shaping the critical narrative. The critical trend solidified in the early modern period, particularly with Jules Michelet (1798–1874), a 19th-century French historian whose Histoire de France (1833–1867) is a landmark in French historiography. Michelet, a romantic nationalist, viewed the Valois monarchy, including John II’s reign, through the lens of France’s struggle for national unity. He criticized John II for his "weakness" and "extravagance," particularly highlighting the Poitiers defeat and the Treaty of Brétigny as catastrophic for French sovereignty. Michelet’s portrayal of John as a well-meaning but ineffectual ruler, overly reliant on favorites like Charles de la Cerda, set a precedent for later historians. His vivid prose and emphasis on national decline made his work highly influential, and he is a likely candidate for initiating the modern trend of criticizing John II. Michelet’s interpretation influenced a chain of historians who cited his work, either directly or indirectly, as they built the critical narrative around John II. Key figures include: 1. François Guizot (1787–1874): A prominent historian and statesman, Guizot’s History of France (1829–1830) drew on Michelet’s framework and Froissart’s chronicles. Guizot emphasized John II’s military failures and the economic devastation caused by the ransom payments, portraying the king as a symbol of feudal incompetence. 2. Charles Petit-Dutaillis (1868–1947): In his The Feudal Monarchy in France and England (1933), Petit-Dutaillis cited Michelet and Guizot, focusing on John II’s inability to centralize royal authority amidst noble defections and English aggression. He described John’s reign as a low point in Valois legitimacy. 3. Edouard Perroy (1901–1974): Perroy’s The Hundred Years War (1945) built on Petit-Dutaillis and Michelet, explicitly citing their works. He criticized John II for his strategic blunders at Poitiers and his failure to manage noble factions, particularly Charles II of Navarre. 4. Jean Deviosse (1920–1992): In Jean le Bon (1985), Deviosse offered a more nuanced view, acknowledging John’s courage and chivalric ideals but still framing his reign as a failure due to the Poitiers debacle and financial mismanagement. Deviosse cited Froissart, Michelet, and Perroy. 5. Maurice Keen (1933–2012): In The Pelican History of Medieval Europe (1969), Keen cited Perroy and Michelet, describing John II as a king overwhelmed by circumstances, with his capture at Poitiers symbolizing the collapse of French royal authority. Recent historians have begun to challenge the critical trend, arguing that John II’s reign must be understood within its medieval context. Françoise Autrand in Charles V: Le Sage (1994) contrasts John’s failures with his son Charles V’s successes but acknowledges John’s efforts to maintain Valois legitimacy amidst unprecedented crises. Autrand cites Deviosse and Froissart but emphasizes the structural challenges—such as the decentralized feudal system and the economic impact of the Black Death—over personal failings. D'Arcy Boulton highlights John II’s establishment of the Order of the Star in 1351 as a bold attempt to strengthen royal authority and unify the French nobility, though he notes its limited success due to political fragmentation and military defeats. Similarly, Georges Bordonove argues that John’s personal bravery, notably in battles such as Poitiers in 1356, and his commitment to chivalric ideals reflect his dedication to royal prestige and the reputation of the Valois. Bordonove further notes that, during his captivity in England, John upheld the dignity of the French crown through his steadfast adherence to honorable conduct despite political and personal adversity.
